facts.content: Reference‑type variables store a reference (address) to an object in memory rather than the actual value.

source_grounding.validation_scope: exact quotation, chunk membership and field coverage only

evidence.quote:
When java runtime environment executes line eight,
 first it's going to allocate some memory to store this point object.
Let's see, the address of that memory location is 100.

Then it's going to allocate a separate part of the memory, and
 it's going to attach this label to that memory location, point 1.

In that memory location, it's going to store the address
 of our point object, so this is the critical difference between primitive
 and reference types.

When we declare a primitive variable like a byte,
 the value that we assign to that variable will be stored in that memory location.

But when we use a reference type, like this point class, our
 variable is going to hold the address of that point object in memory,
 not the actual point object.
